text: SQL injection and cross-site scripting both trace back to the exact same root cause: a web application took data a user typed in and used it directly, without checking or cleaning it first, somewhere that data could change how the application behaves. That single mistake, trusting input instead of validating it, is behind an enormous share of real-world web breaches, which is why input validation sits at the top of nearly every web security framework, including the OWASP Top 10.

SQL injection happens when unsanitized user input gets inserted directly into a database query, letting an attacker alter the query's logic rather than its data. Cross-site scripting, or XSS, happens when an attacker gets malicious script injected into a page so it executes inside other users' browsers, not the attacker's own. Different target, same cause: input that should have been treated as data got trusted as something safe to run.

Walk through SQL injection conceptually: a login form pastes whatever a user types directly into its database query with no checking. A carefully crafted string in that field can change the query's logic itself, for example making a password check evaluate as true regardless of the actual password. The attacker never guesses a password — they manipulate the query. The fix is parameterized queries, which keep a query's structure completely separate from the data plugged into it.

XSS works the same way in a different place: a comment field stores exactly what a user submits and displays it back to every visitor without sanitizing it. If an attacker submits script instead of plain text, and the page renders it as live code, that script runs in every viewer's browser with that browser's own trust in the site intact. The fix is output encoding — treating submitted content as data to display, never as code to execute.

Up next, in Chapter 7: defense in depth and the security layered model — how all the attack types from this chapter get countered not by one control, but by multiple overlapping layers of defense working together.
